metric.why: Announced megawatts are the leading indicator for land, power, and equipment demand. The published numbers come almost entirely from commercial research firms; this site links to who publishes them rather than republishing figures it cannot verify.
metric.definition: Capacity in permitting, planned, or under construction per market, the standard unit for comparing data center booms across regions.

reading.body:
The construction pipeline in megawatts is the leading indicator of data center demand for land, power, and equipment, but the published figures come from commercial research firms rather than independent verification.

The metric counts capacity that is in permitting, planned, or under construction, broken out by market. It measures intent and early commitment, not operating capacity. Megawatts are the standard unit for comparing regional booms because power, not floor space, is what constrains a data center. Two markets with similar land and capital can differ entirely in how much electricity they can actually secure.

For AI this is the earliest stage at which power becomes the binding constraint. A pipeline figure is a claim on grid interconnection, transformers, and land before any of it is built, so it moves ahead of the equipment orders and construction spending that follow. If the pipeline is the leading indicator, then the grid and the permitting process sit upstream of everything the AI buildout is usually measured by.

What the data does not provide is any actual number. There are no megawatt totals, no markets, no dates, and no split between permitted, planned, and under construction. It defines the metric and flags that its sourcing is commercial research rather than audited disclosure. It also cannot say how much of any announced pipeline gets built, how long permitting takes, or whether the announced capacity has secured power at all. Announced is not built, and this data does not close that gap.
